A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniOcc and contain matching datasets, framework components and core experiments. Their text, equations, figures and tables are readable. Inspection of both complete PDFs, including v2's supplementary material, supports reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of flow-augmented OccWorld, cross-source training, camera-based occupancy prediction and cooperative prediction in Tables 3–6.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical evaluations and adds object-level-flow comparisons, real-only mixed-source training results and highway-focused CARLA experiments.

M1.justification: Supplementary Section 7.3 introduces an ego-localization procedure that estimates rigid transformations from static-voxel flows using Kabsch and RANSAC, inverts them into ego motion and accumulates poses. This substantially extends the processing toolkit. The existing OccWorld flow encoder, cross-attention fusion, decoder and L2 supervision remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The four data sources and principal occupancy tasks remain. v2 adds training and evaluation involving highway-focused CARLA scenes generated with Town06, supporting speeds up to 55 mph (Section 8, Table 6). This extends the represented driving conditions within the existing simulation domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds an object-level-flow OccWorld comparator alongside no flow and voxel-level flow on both nuScenes and Waymo (Tables 2 and 8). v1 Table 3 compared only with and without voxel flow. Cam4DOcc, CVTOcc and CoHFF remain in their corresponding evaluations.

E3.justification: v2 adds nuScenes-plus-Waymo-only training configurations, a standard-versus-highway CARLA comparison, and evaluation through a weighted UniOcc Score (Section 9). These supplement the existing protocol; the stated 200×200×16 grid, 0.4 m resolution and three-second observation/forecast horizons remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new object-flow comparisons test whether fine-grained voxel motion offers benefits beyond coarse object motion. Section 8 adds a substantive investigation of simulation–real compatibility through speed-distribution histograms and highway-scene training experiments. These directly examine two central explanations behind the benchmark's reported benefits.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added GMM-fitting and RANSAC details describe algorithm computation rather than uncertainty reporting for experimental performance.

E6.justification: v2 adds object-flow, real-only mixed-training, highway-training and composite-score results in Tables 2, 3, 6, 8 and 9. It also changes same-source Pcar values from 75.52 to 82.57 for nuScenes and 71.23 to 86.68 for Waymo between v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 3, resolving discrepancies with v1's flow table. Other retained benchmark values match.

T1.justification: v2 substantially extends the mathematical development with explicit dynamic/static flow transformations, rigid-registration and inverse-ego-motion derivations under a static-scene assumption, and a formal definition of the composite UniOcc Score (Sections 7 and 9). The original tracking and individual evaluation equations remain; no new theorem or proof is presented.

C1.justification: The introduction adds an explicit Python-toolkit contribution whose scope includes localization, detection, tracking, alignment and visualization, and the abstract now emphasizes the toolkit. The central claims about unified data, voxel-level flows, cooperative support and ground-truth-free evaluation otherwise remain.

C2.justification: v1 Section 4.3 broadly emphasizes benefits across domains and improved background forecasting. v2 qualifies this interpretation: its generalization discussion focuses on mixing real datasets, while simulation mixing can degrade temporal consistency. It explicitly discusses the already-reported nuScenes IoUbg decrease from 59.56 to 55.07 and investigates speed mismatch as a potential explanation in Section 8.

D1.justification: v2 supplies previously undocumented flow-computation formulas, GMM fitting with EM/BIC selection over 1–20 components and four covariance types, voxel-scale perturbations, PCA pseudocode and tracking-distance thresholds. It also specifies localization's RANSAC threshold and iteration limit. These substantially improve technical disclosure without establishing changes to existing experiments. Data/code access instructions switch from direct dataset/repository links to a project website.

R1.justification: Section 2.5 and the expanded supplementary Broader Impacts substantially broaden connections to trajectory prediction, aerial–ground collaboration, point-cloud completion, vision-language models and generative world models. Added references include AirV2X, LangCoop and TrajEvo; STAMP is removed. The principal positioning against existing occupancy benchmarks remains.

P1.justification: Main Sections 1–5 retain their order and much of their wording. Editing concentrates on the abstract and contribution list, the rewritten and reordered Section 4.3 discussion, expanded Broader Impacts moved into the supplement, and explanatory cross-references. This is localized restructuring rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 gains a distinct toolkit stage, Figure 2 is redrawn, and Figure 6's existing examples are rearranged. New supplementary diagrams, speed histograms, pseudocode and result tables substantially expand the presentation. The label table moves to the supplement, and the original flow comparison is split between main-text and supplementary tables.

improvement.justification: The flow-granularity controls and simulation-speed investigation strengthen previously incomplete support for central arguments. Section 7 substantially improves methodological transparency, while Sections 4.3 and 8 replace overly broad simulation-benefit interpretations with evidence-based qualifications. Together these materially improve the benchmark's credibility and usefulness. The new composite score has a limited reporting defect—its weights sum to 1.10 despite being described as a weighted average—but this does not outweigh those gains.
